description: Notebooks are themselves Wolfram Language expressions, so documents, cells and interactive interfaces can be created and manipulated programmatically. This category covers the dynamic interactivity framework (Manipulate, Dynamic, controls), the layout and styling constructs used to arrange output, the notebook manipulation functions, and the output forms used to convert expressions to TeX, C and traditional mathematical notation.

tools.name: Manipulate
tools.description: Creates an interactive interface with automatically generated controls for the specified variables, re-evaluating the expression whenever a control changes. Each variable specification {u, min, max} produces a slider, a list of values produces a popup or setter bar, and {u, {True, False}} produces a checkbox. It is the fastest way to explore how a result depends on parameters.
tools.usage:
Manipulate[expr, {u, umin, umax}]
Manipulate[expr, {u, umin, umax, du}]
Manipulate[expr, {{u, init, "label"}, umin, umax}]
Manipulate[expr, {u, {v1, v2, ...}}]

parameters.name: ControlType
parameters.description: Force a particular control, e.g. Slider, PopupMenu, SetterBar, InputField, Checkbox.

parameters.name: Initialization
parameters.description: Code evaluated once before the interface is first displayed.

parameters.name: TrackedSymbols
parameters.description: Restrict which symbols trigger an update, avoiding unnecessary recomputation.

tools.example:
Manipulate[Plot[Sin[a x], {x, 0, 2 Pi}], {a, 1, 5}]
Manipulate[n!, {n, 1, 20, 1}]
Manipulate[Plot[f[x], {x, 0, 10}], {f, {Sin, Cos, Tan}}]
Manipulate[Graphics[Circle[{0, 0}, r]], {{r, 1, "radius"}, 0.1, 3}]
tools.notes: Everything inside Manipulate is held and localized like DynamicModule, so outer variables must be injected with With. Use ControlActive or a coarser step to keep dragging responsive for expensive computations.

tools.name: Dynamic
tools.description: Displays an expression that automatically updates whenever any of the symbols it depends on changes. It is the low-level reactivity primitive on which Manipulate and all the controls are built. The displayed value is recomputed in the front end, so Dynamic output is live rather than a snapshot.
tools.usage:
Dynamic[expr]
Dynamic[expr, TrackedSymbols :> {x}]
Dynamic[x, (x = #) &]
tools.notes: Dynamic is HoldFirst, so a variable used inside it must be in scope when the output is displayed; use With to insert fixed values. Excessive Dynamic expressions slow the front end noticeably.

tools.name: DynamicModule
tools.description: Creates variables local to a displayed output expression, so each copy of an interface keeps its own independent state that persists across evaluations and notebook saves. It is the scoping construct for interactive interfaces, analogous to Module for ordinary code. Manipulate wraps its variables in a DynamicModule automatically.
tools.usage:
DynamicModule[{x = x0, ...}, expr]
DynamicModule[vars, expr, Initialization :> code]
tools.example:
DynamicModule[{n = 0}, Column[{Button["increment", n++], Dynamic[n]}]]
DynamicModule[{pts = {}}, EventHandler[Graphics[Dynamic[Point[pts]], PlotRange -> 1], {"MouseClicked" :> AppendTo[pts, MousePosition["Graphics"]]}]]
DynamicModule[{x = 1}, Slider[Dynamic[x]]]
tools.notes: State in a DynamicModule survives being saved in a notebook, which is what makes self-contained interactive documents possible.

tools.name: Control
tools.description: Generates the control object that Manipulate would create for a given variable specification, so it can be placed anywhere in a custom layout. It takes the same {{var, init, label}, min, max} specifications as Manipulate. Use it when you need full control over the arrangement of an interface.
tools.usage:
Control[{u, umin, umax}]
Control[{{u, init, label}, umin, umax}]
Control[{u, {v1, v2}}]
tools.example:
DynamicModule[{a = 1}, Column[{Control[{{a, 1, "gain"}, 0, 5}], Dynamic[Plot[a Sin[x], {x, 0, 2 Pi}]]}]]
Control[{x, 0, 1}]
Control[{c, {Red, Green, Blue}}]

tools.name: Slider
tools.description: A draggable slider control bound to a Dynamic variable, with an optional {min, max, step} range specification. Slider2D gives a two-dimensional pad returning a coordinate pair, and IntervalSlider selects a range. Sliders are the default control Manipulate creates for a numeric range.
tools.usage:
Slider[Dynamic[x]]
Slider[Dynamic[x], {min, max}]
Slider[Dynamic[x], {min, max, step}]
Slider2D[Dynamic[pt]]
tools.example:
DynamicModule[{x = 0.5}, {Slider[Dynamic[x]], Dynamic[x]}]
Slider[Dynamic[n], {1, 10, 1}]
DynamicModule[{p = {0, 0}}, {Slider2D[Dynamic[p]], Dynamic[p]}]
Slider[Dynamic[v], {0, 100}, ImageSize -> 300]

tools.name: Button
tools.description: A clickable button that evaluates an action when pressed; the action is held until the click occurs. The Method -> "Queued" option runs the action in the kernel rather than in the front end, which is required for anything long-running or that prints. Buttons are the basic trigger for imperative actions in an interface.
tools.usage:
Button[label, action]
Button[label, action, Method -> "Queued"]
Button[label, action, Appearance -> "Palette"]
tools.example:
DynamicModule[{n = 0}, Column[{Button["count", n++], Dynamic[n]}]]
Button["compute", result = Integrate[f, x], Method -> "Queued"]
Button["open", SystemOpen[file]]
Button["reset", pts = {}]
tools.notes: Without Method -> "Queued" the action runs in the front end and long computations freeze the interface.

tools.name: Checkbox
tools.description: A toggle control bound to a Dynamic variable, True when checked and False otherwise. A second argument supplies a list of values to cycle through instead of booleans. Manipulate creates a Checkbox automatically for a variable declared as {u, {True, False}}.
tools.usage:
Checkbox[Dynamic[x]]
Checkbox[Dynamic[x], {val1, val2}]
CheckboxBar[Dynamic[list], {v1, v2, ...}]
tools.example:
DynamicModule[{on = False}, {Checkbox[Dynamic[on]], Dynamic[on]}]
Manipulate[Plot[Sin[x], {x, 0, Pi}, Frame -> f], {f, {True, False}}]
CheckboxBar[Dynamic[sel], {"a", "b", "c"}]

tools.name: PopupMenu
tools.description: A dropdown menu control bound to a Dynamic variable, choosing among a list of values or of value -> label rules. It is the control Manipulate generates for a variable with many discrete choices. ActionMenu is the variant whose items run actions instead of setting a value.
tools.usage:
PopupMenu[Dynamic[x], {v1, v2, ...}]
PopupMenu[Dynamic[x], {v1 -> lbl1, v2 -> lbl2}]
ActionMenu[label, {lbl :> action, ...}]
tools.example:
DynamicModule[{c = Red}, {PopupMenu[Dynamic[c], {Red, Green, Blue}], Dynamic[Graphics[{c, Disk[]}, ImageSize -> 50]]}]
PopupMenu[Dynamic[m], {"linear" -> "Linear fit", "quad" -> "Quadratic fit"}]
ActionMenu["file", {"open" :> open[], "save" :> save[]}]

tools.name: RadioButtonBar
tools.description: A row of radio buttons for choosing one value from a small set, bound to a Dynamic variable. SetterBar gives the same behaviour with a segmented-button appearance, and TogglerBar allows multiple selection. All three take values or value -> label rules.
tools.usage:
RadioButtonBar[Dynamic[x], {v1, v2, ...}]
SetterBar[Dynamic[x], {v1 -> lbl1, ...}]
TogglerBar[Dynamic[list], {v1, v2}]
tools.example:
DynamicModule[{mode = "a"}, {RadioButtonBar[Dynamic[mode], {"a", "b", "c"}], Dynamic[mode]}]
SetterBar[Dynamic[n], Range[5]]
TogglerBar[Dynamic[opts], {"grid", "frame", "legend"}]

tools.name: InputField
tools.description: A text or expression input box bound to a Dynamic variable, with a type argument choosing between Expression, String and Number interpretation. The value updates when the field loses focus or Enter is pressed. It is the control to use when a value cannot be picked from a range or a list.
tools.usage:
InputField[Dynamic[x]]
InputField[Dynamic[x], String]
InputField[Dynamic[x], Number]
tools.example:
DynamicModule[{s = ""}, {InputField[Dynamic[s], String], Dynamic[StringLength[s]]}]
InputField[Dynamic[n], Number, FieldSize -> 5]
Manipulate[f[x], {{x, 1}, InputField}]

tools.name: Animate
tools.description: Creates an animated version of Manipulate that advances a variable automatically over its range, with play, pause and speed controls. AnimationRate and DefaultDuration control the pace, and AnimationRunning -> False starts it paused. ListAnimate animates a precomputed list of frames, which is smoother for expensive graphics.
tools.usage:
Animate[expr, {u, umin, umax}]
Animate[expr, {u, umin, umax, du}]
ListAnimate[{frame1, frame2, ...}]
tools.example:
Animate[Plot[Sin[x + t], {x, 0, 2 Pi}], {t, 0, 2 Pi}]
Animate[Graphics[Disk[{Cos[t], Sin[t]}, 0.1], PlotRange -> 1.5], {t, 0, 2 Pi}, AnimationRate -> 0.5]
ListAnimate[Table[Plot[Sin[n x], {x, 0, Pi}], {n, 1, 5}]]
tools.notes: Precomputing frames into a list and using ListAnimate avoids recomputation on every frame and gives much smoother playback.

tools.name: EventHandler
tools.description: Attaches handlers for mouse and keyboard events to any displayed expression, so clicks, drags and key presses can run arbitrary code. Event names include "MouseClicked", "MouseDragged", "MouseMoved", "KeyDown" and specific key strings. It is the way to build custom interactive graphics beyond what the standard controls offer.
tools.usage:
EventHandler[expr, {"event" :> action}]
EventHandler[expr, {"MouseClicked" :> act, "KeyDown" :> act2}]
tools.example:
DynamicModule[{pts = {}}, EventHandler[Dynamic[Graphics[Point[pts], PlotRange -> 1]], {"MouseClicked" :> AppendTo[pts, MousePosition["Graphics"]]}]]
EventHandler[Style["click me", 20], {"MouseClicked" :> Print["clicked"]}]
EventHandler[Dynamic[n], {{"KeyDown", "a"} :> n++}]

tools.name: Refresh
tools.description: Controls when a Dynamic expression recomputes: UpdateInterval forces periodic refresh by wall clock, and TrackedSymbols restricts which symbol changes trigger it. It is the tool for clocks, polling displays and for suppressing unwanted updates in a complex interface. None as the tracked symbol list means the expression updates only on the timer.
tools.usage:
Refresh[expr, UpdateInterval -> t]
Refresh[expr, TrackedSymbols :> {x}]
Refresh[expr, None]
tools.example:
Dynamic[Refresh[DateString[], UpdateInterval -> 1]]
Dynamic[Refresh[expensivePlot[a, b], TrackedSymbols :> {a}]]
Dynamic[Refresh[RandomReal[], UpdateInterval -> 0.5]]

tools.name: Row
tools.description: Lays out a list of expressions horizontally, optionally with a separator string or expression between them. It is the simplest way to combine several outputs on one line, including a mixture of text, numbers and graphics. Spacer gives explicit horizontal gaps.
tools.usage:
Row[{e1, e2, ...}]
Row[list, separator]
tools.example:
Row[{"x = ", 5}]
Row[{plot1, plot2}]
Row[{"a", "b", "c"}, ", "]
Row[{img, Spacer[20], caption}]

tools.name: Column
tools.description: Stacks a list of expressions vertically with optional alignment, spacing and dividers. It is the counterpart of Row and is often used to build simple interfaces and reports. Alignment options accept Left, Center, Right or a list per column.
tools.usage:
Column[{e1, e2, ...}]
Column[list, alignment]
Column[list, Dividers -> All, Spacings -> 2]
tools.example:
Column[{"Title", plot, "caption"}]
Column[{1, 22, 333}, Right]
Column[{Slider[Dynamic[x]], Dynamic[x]}]
Column[rows, Dividers -> All]

tools.name: Grid
tools.description: Arranges a nested list into a two-dimensional grid with detailed control over frames, alignment, spacing, backgrounds and spanning items. SpanFromLeft and SpanFromAbove merge cells. It is the general layout function for tables, forms and dashboards, and unlike TableForm its output is a normal expression that can be styled and nested.
tools.usage:
Grid[{{a, b}, {c, d}}]
Grid[data, Frame -> All]
Grid[data, Alignment -> Left, Background -> {None, {LightGray, White}}]
Grid[data, Dividers -> All]

parameters.name: Frame
parameters.description: All, None, or detailed per-row/column specifications.

parameters.name: Alignment
parameters.description: Left, Center, Right, or {columns, rows} specifications.

parameters.name: Background
parameters.description: Colors for cells, rows or columns, supporting alternating patterns.

parameters.name: ItemSize
parameters.description: Fixed or automatic sizing of grid items.

tools.example:
Grid[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}, Frame -> All]
Grid[Prepend[data, {"name", "value"}], Dividers -> {False, {2 -> True}}]
Grid[{{"merged", SpanFromLeft}, {1, 2}}, Frame -> All]
Grid[Table[i j, {i, 3}, {j, 3}], Alignment -> Right]

tools.name: Pane
tools.description: Displays an expression inside a region of fixed size, adding scrollbars or clipping when the content is larger. It is how you keep a long output or a wide table from expanding the whole notebook. ImageSizeAction controls whether content is scrolled, clipped or shrunk to fit.
tools.usage:
Pane[expr, size]
Pane[expr, {w, h}]
Pane[expr, size, Scrollbars -> True]
tools.example:
Pane[Range[1000], {300, 100}, Scrollbars -> True]
Pane[longText, 400]
Pane[Grid[bigData], {500, 200}, Scrollbars -> Automatic]

tools.name: Panel
tools.description: Displays an expression inside a styled panel with a background and border matching the system look, optionally with a heading. It groups related interface elements visually and is commonly used around control clusters. Framed is the simpler alternative when only a plain border is wanted.
tools.usage:
Panel[expr]
Panel[expr, heading]
Panel[expr, heading, Alignment -> Left]
tools.example:
Panel[Column[{Slider[Dynamic[x]], Dynamic[x]}]]
Panel[plot, "Temperature over time"]
Panel[Grid[data, Frame -> All], "Results"]

tools.name: Framed
tools.description: Draws a frame around an expression, with options for the frame style, background, rounding and internal padding. It is the lightest-weight way to visually separate output. FrameStyle and RoundingRadius give control over its appearance.
tools.usage:
Framed[expr]
Framed[expr, FrameStyle -> style]
Framed[expr, Background -> color, RoundingRadius -> r]
tools.example:
Framed["important"]
Framed[plot, FrameStyle -> Directive[Thick, Red]]
Framed[Column[items], Background -> LightYellow, RoundingRadius -> 5]

tools.name: Style
tools.description: Applies font, size, color, weight and other display directives to an expression without changing its value for computation. It accepts named style sheet names such as "Section" or "Text" as well as explicit directives like Bold, Italic, 16 and Red. Style is the standard way to format labels, plot annotations and report text.
tools.usage:
Style[expr, options]
Style[expr, size]
Style[expr, color, Bold]
Style[expr, "StyleName"]
tools.example:
Style["Title", 24, Bold]
Style[x^2, Red, Italic]
Style["warning", FontFamily -> "Helvetica", FontColor -> Orange]
Plot[Sin[x], {x, 0, Pi}, PlotLabel -> Style["sine", 16, Bold]]
tools.notes: Style is purely a display wrapper: Style[2, Red] + 3 still evaluates to 5 wrapped in Style, so strip it before numeric comparisons if needed.

tools.name: Text
tools.description: Marks an expression as text so it is displayed in the text style rather than in mathematical typesetting, and inside Graphics it places a text label at a coordinate. Graphics usage takes optional offset and direction arguments for precise placement. It is the primitive behind plot labels and annotations.
tools.usage:
Text[expr]
Text[expr, coords]
Text[expr, coords, offset]
Text[expr, coords, offset, direction]
tools.example:
Text["some prose"]
Graphics[{Text["origin", {0, 0}], Point[{0, 0}]}]
Graphics[{Text[Style["A", 16], {1, 1}, {0, -1}]}]
Graphics[{Text["rotated", {0, 0}, {0, 0}, {0, 1}]}]

tools.name: Labeled
tools.description: Attaches a label to an expression, placed above, below or to either side according to a position specification. It is the clean way to caption a plot or annotate a control without building a Grid. Several labels with different positions can be attached at once.
tools.usage:
Labeled[expr, label]
Labeled[expr, label, pos]
Labeled[expr, {l1, l2}, {pos1, pos2}]
tools.example:
Labeled[Plot[Sin[x], {x, 0, Pi}], "sine wave"]
Labeled[slider, "gain", Left]
Labeled[chart, {"Title", "source: data.csv"}, {Top, Bottom}]
Labeled[img, Style["Figure 1", Bold], Bottom]

tools.name: Tooltip
tools.description: Shows an auxiliary expression when the mouse hovers over the displayed object, without changing the object itself. It works on graphics primitives, chart elements and ordinary output, making it the easiest way to add interactive detail to a visualization. Many chart functions accept Tooltip in their data automatically.
tools.usage:
Tooltip[expr, label]
Tooltip[expr]
tools.example:
Tooltip[Style["hover me", 16], "extra detail"]
Graphics[{Tooltip[Disk[{0, 0}, 1], "unit disk"]}]
ListPlot[Tooltip /@ data]
BarChart[{Tooltip[3, "A"], Tooltip[5, "B"]}]

tools.name: Mouseover
tools.description: Displays one expression normally and a different one while the mouse is over the region. It is used for hover highlighting, revealing extra information, and simple interactive figures. Unlike Tooltip the alternate content replaces the original in place rather than appearing in a floating box.
tools.usage: Mouseover[expr1, expr2]
tools.example:
Mouseover["off", Style["on", Red, Bold]]
Graphics[{Mouseover[{Blue, Disk[]}, {Red, Disk[]}]}]
Mouseover[thumbnail, fullImage]

tools.name: Placed
tools.description: Specifies where a label, legend or other element should be positioned within a graphic or layout construct. It is most often used with PlotLegends and with Labeled to move a legend inside the plot area or to a named corner. Position specifications include Above, Below, Left, Right, Center and scaled coordinates.
tools.usage:
Placed[expr, pos]
PlotLegends -> Placed[legend, pos]
Labeled[expr, Placed[label, pos]]
tools.example:
Plot[{Sin[x], Cos[x]}, {x, 0, 2 Pi}, PlotLegends -> Placed[{"sin", "cos"}, Below]]
BarChart[data, ChartLegends -> Placed[labels, Right]]
Plot[Sin[x], {x, 0, Pi}, PlotLegends -> Placed["sine", {0.8, 0.8}]]

tools.name: Cell
tools.description: Represents a single notebook cell, with its contents, style name and options. Notebooks are lists of Cell expressions, so generating a document programmatically amounts to building Cell objects. Styles include "Input", "Output", "Text", "Section", "Title" and any style defined in the stylesheet.
tools.usage:
Cell[contents, "style"]
Cell[contents, "style", options]
Cell[BoxData[boxes], "Input"]
TextCell[expr, "style"]
tools.example:
Cell["Introduction", "Section"]
Cell["Some explanatory text.", "Text"]
Cell[BoxData[ToBoxes[Plot[Sin[x], {x, 0, Pi}]]], "Output"]
TextCell["quick text cell", "Text"]
tools.notes: ExpressionCell and TextCell are convenience constructors that handle the box conversion for you.

tools.name: CellPrint
tools.description: Inserts one or more cells into the current notebook below the cell being evaluated. Unlike Print, which creates a plain print cell, CellPrint lets you choose the style and options of the generated cell. It is the way to emit headings, formatted text or new input cells from running code.
tools.usage:
CellPrint[cell]
CellPrint[{cell1, cell2}]
CellPrint[TextCell[expr, "style"]]
tools.example:
CellPrint[Cell["Results", "Section"]]
CellPrint[TextCell["Analysis complete.", "Text"]]
CellPrint[ExpressionCell[Defer[Plot[Sin[x], {x, 0, Pi}]], "Input"]]

tools.name: Notebook
tools.description: Represents an entire notebook as a Wolfram Language expression: a list of Cell objects together with notebook-level options such as StyleDefinitions and WindowSize. Because a notebook is just an expression, whole documents can be generated, transformed and exported programmatically. NotebookPut displays such an expression as a live notebook.
tools.usage:
Notebook[{cell1, cell2, ...}]
Notebook[cells, options]
NotebookPut[nbexpr]
NotebookGet[nbobj]

tools.name: CreateDocument
tools.description: Creates and displays a new notebook containing the given expressions, each placed in its own cell. It is the quickest way to generate a report window from code without assembling a full Notebook expression. Options control the window title, style sheet and visibility.
tools.usage:
CreateDocument[]
CreateDocument[expr]
CreateDocument[{expr1, expr2}]
CreateDocument[cells, opts]
tools.example:
CreateDocument[{TextCell["Summary", "Section"], plot, TextCell["Details", "Text"]}]
CreateDocument[Plot[Sin[x], {x, 0, 2 Pi}]]
nb = CreateDocument[]; NotebookWrite[nb, Cell["hello", "Text"]];
CreateDocument[content, WindowTitle -> "Report"]

tools.name: NotebookWrite
tools.description: Writes cells or expressions into a notebook at the current selection, replacing whatever is selected. Together with SelectionMove and NotebookFind it supports programmatic editing of a live document. The notebook is specified by a NotebookObject such as the one returned by CreateDocument or EvaluationNotebook[].
tools.usage:
NotebookWrite[nbobj, data]
NotebookWrite[nbobj, data, selection]
SelectionMove[nbobj, Next, Cell]

tools.name: NotebookPut
tools.description: Takes a Notebook expression and opens it as a live notebook in the front end, returning a NotebookObject. NotebookGet performs the reverse, converting an open notebook back into an expression. This pair is the foundation of programmatic document generation and transformation.
tools.usage:
NotebookPut[nbexpr]
NotebookPut[nbexpr, nbobj]
NotebookGet[nbobj]

tools.name: NotebookEvaluate
tools.description: Evaluates all the input cells of a notebook file or open notebook and returns the value of the last one. InsertResults -> True writes the outputs back into the notebook, which makes it a batch runner for computational documents. It is how a notebook is executed non-interactively from a script.
tools.usage:
NotebookEvaluate["file.nb"]
NotebookEvaluate[nbobj]
NotebookEvaluate["file.nb", InsertResults -> True]
tools.example:
NotebookEvaluate["analysis.nb"]
NotebookEvaluate["report.nb", InsertResults -> True]
nb = NotebookOpen["calc.nb"]; NotebookEvaluate[nb]
tools.notes: Under wolframscript a front end is still required for notebook evaluation; use `wolframscript -file` with a .wl script when no front end is available.

tools.name: TraditionalForm
tools.description: Displays an expression in conventional mathematical notation, with f(x) instead of f[x], integrals with dx and standard special function symbols. It is for presentation only; input in TraditionalForm is ambiguous and should be avoided. StandardForm is the unambiguous two-dimensional form used by default in notebooks.
tools.usage:
TraditionalForm[expr]
expr // TraditionalForm
StandardForm[expr]
tools.example:
TraditionalForm[Integrate[x^2, x]]
TraditionalForm[BesselJ[0, x]]
Plot[Sin[x], {x, 0, Pi}, PlotLabel -> TraditionalForm[Sin[x]]]
x^2/y // TraditionalForm
tools.notes: Copying TraditionalForm output back as input often produces a different expression, because the notation is not one to one.

tools.name: TeXForm
tools.description: Converts an expression to a LaTeX string representing the same mathematics, which can be pasted into a paper or a Markdown document. ToString[expr, TeXForm] gives the plain string rather than the formatted object. The inverse direction is available with ToExpression[str, TeXForm].
tools.usage:
TeXForm[expr]
ToString[expr, TeXForm]
ToExpression["latex", TeXForm]
tools.example:
TeXForm[Integrate[x^2, x]]
ToString[Sqrt[x^2 + y^2], TeXForm]
TeXForm[Sum[1/n^2, {n, 1, Infinity}]]
ToExpression["\\frac{a}{b}", TeXForm]

tools.name: CForm
tools.description: Converts an expression to a C language expression string, translating powers, elementary functions and constants into their C equivalents. FortranForm does the same for Fortran. Both are useful for exporting a symbolic result into generated source code, though for serious code generation the Wolfram compiler and CCodeGenerator are more complete.
tools.usage:
CForm[expr]
FortranForm[expr]
ToString[expr, CForm]
tools.example:
CForm[x^2 + Sqrt[y]]
CForm[D[Sin[x] Exp[x], x]]
FortranForm[a x^2 + b x + c]
ToString[CForm[expr]]
tools.notes: CForm writes Power(x,2) rather than x*x and does not declare variables; treat it as a starting point rather than compilable code.

tools.name: TableForm
tools.description: Displays a list or nested list as a table with optional row and column headings. Like MatrixForm it is a formatting wrapper, not a data structure, so do not assign its output to a variable used in computation. Grid is the more flexible modern alternative with full control over frames and styling.
tools.usage:
TableForm[list]
TableForm[list, TableHeadings -> {rows, cols}]
TableForm[list, TableDepth -> n]
tools.example:
TableForm[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}]
TableForm[data, TableHeadings -> {None, {"x", "y"}}]
TableForm[Table[{n, n^2}, {n, 5}], TableHeadings -> {None, {"n", "n^2"}}]
TableForm[assoc]

tools.name: Rasterize
tools.description: Converts any displayed expression, including formatted output and interfaces, into an Image or raster graphic at a specified resolution. It is used to freeze a dynamic interface into a static picture, to embed formatted output in a report, and to measure rendered sizes. Requesting the "BoundingBox" element gives the rendered dimensions without the image.
tools.usage:
Rasterize[expr]
Rasterize[expr, "Image"]
Rasterize[expr, ImageResolution -> n]
Rasterize[expr, "BoundingBox"]
tools.example:
Rasterize[Plot[Sin[x], {x, 0, Pi}]]
img = Rasterize[Grid[data, Frame -> All], ImageResolution -> 200];
Export["table.png", img]
Rasterize[Style["text", 30], "BoundingBox"]
tools.notes: Rasterize requires a front end; in a headless kernel use Export to an image format instead, which renders graphics without rasterizing typeset output.
